newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asian Grain - Japan to step up soybean purchases.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grain - Japan to step up soybean purchases.

text.p: Japan will step up purchases of U.S. and Brazilian soybeans this week ahead of the Christmas holidays, as it trys to cover about half of its February requirements by the end of the week, traders said on Monday.

Buyers from Taiwan could hold a tender for a combined shipment of 54,000 tonnes of U.S. corn and soybeans while those from South Korea and the Philippines will probably be sidelined due to the seasonal lull induced by the holiday period.
"We'd like to cover U.S. soybeans for nearly 50 percent of February shipments by the end of this week," one Tokyo-based trader said.
Japanese premiums for U.S. soybeans are quoted at around 130 U.S. cents a bushel over the Chicago Board of Trade's (CBOT) March contract.

Japan has already purchased more than 300,000 tonnes of Brazilian soybeans for April-June 1997 shipment, traders said, adding that Japan could also buy U.S. corn for April-June 1997 shipment this week.

"Firming freight rates have motivated some feed makers to buy U.S. corn," a trader said. The U.S. Gulf/Japan freight rate is currently quoted at US$25.75 a tonne against a quote of around $19 a tonne a few months back.
"But Japanese buyers are watching price differences between U.S. and Argentine corn," another corn trader said.
Some trading houses in Japan are gradually stepping up corn import talks for 1997 with Argentina following a grain mission to the South American country.
In Taiwan, Hui Shung may tender for U.S. corn and soybeans while other buyers may follow its lead if it gets a good price within the next two weeks.
Dealers said the new South American soybean crop also bears watching.
"The South American crop should start to put pressure on the U.S. market in late January," a soybean trader said.
South Korean grains and oilseeds buyers are likely to hold back their purchases until January because of the traditional slowdown of business at this time of the year, traders said.
Most of the buyers are also in no hurry because they have ample stocks booked for delivery early next year, they said.

"We believe buyers will take a back seat until January since they are in a low-key period and have no need to hurry (their) purchases," an official with Korea's National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF) said.

In January, several groups are expected to buy 15,000 tonnes of soymeal for delivery by March 20 to Kunsan, and the Korea Feed Association is likely to buy about 30,000 tonnes of soymeal for delivery by March 10 to Inchon and Ulsan, traders said.
The NLCF official said corn buyers would probably stay out of the market until early February as they appeared to be well covered for most of their needs.

He said freight premiums remain firm at $13 to $14 a tonne from the Pacific Northwest and $23 a tonne from the U.S. Gulf. Premiums are holding on expectations that demand for grains will gain momentum in the near future.
Philippine buyers will also probably sit it out but were poised to buy on the dips, flour company officials said.
"If prices soften next week, we can buy for our January requirement," one miller said.
The price of the March contract in Minneapolis, where the Philippines buys most of its wheat, slipped 2-1/4 U.S. cents on Friday to close at $3.85 a bushel.
"We may see more purchases from other countries like Canada, Australia and Argentina if U.S. prices don't soften for the rest of the year," another Manila-based flour mill executive said.
